findings.title: Options-object construction silently enables rejectOnClear by default
findings.cause: When the input is an options object, destructuring uses `rejectOnClear = true` even though the top-level default and public API document the default as false.
findings.impact: `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` behaves differently from `pLimit(1)`: `clearQueue()` rejects pending promises with AbortError instead of leaving them pending/discarded. This is a contract mismatch for users adopting the documented options-object form without explicitly opting into rejection.
findings.evidence: index.js:4 initializes `rejectOnClear` to false, but index.js:6-8 overwrites omitted object values with true. readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 state `rejectOnClear` default is false. Runtime probe printed {"pendingCount":0,"settled":true,"outcome":["rejected","AbortError","This operation was aborted"]} after `pLimit({concurrency: 1}).clearQueue()` on a pending task.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `node --input-type=module` with: import pLimit from "./index.js"; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const first = limit(() => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 50))); const second = limit(() => "second"); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); second.then(v => console.log("fulfilled", v), e => console.log("rejected", e.name)); await first; Expected under docs: pending promise is not rejected unless rejectOnClear is explicitly true. Actual: rejected AbortError.

findings.title: limitFunction drops every argument passed to the limited wrapper
findings.cause: `limitFunction` returns a zero-argument wrapper and invokes `function_()` without forwarding the wrapper call arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on parameters receives `undefined` values at runtime, despite the TypeScript signature returning `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. This breaks normal use cases such as limiting a request helper, mapper, or keyed operation.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 implements `return () => limit(() => function_());`. index.d.ts:133-136 promises that the returned function accepts the same argument tuple as the source function. Runtime probe `limited("alpha", "beta")` returned `undefined:undefined` for an async `(value, suffix) => `${value}:${suffix}`` function.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `node --input-type=module` with: import {limitFunction} from "./index.js"; const limited = limitFunction(async (value, suffix) => `${value}:${suffix}`, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited("alpha", "beta")); Expected: `alpha:beta`. Actual: `undefined:undefined`.

findings.title: limit.map passes undefined as the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: `map` detects arrays and only forwards the Array.from index for arrays; all other iterables receive `undefined` as the second mapper argument.
findings.impact: The API claims support for arbitrary iterables and says the mapper receives `(item, index)`. Set, generator, and iterator inputs lose the index, causing incorrect output for mapper functions that rely on documented positional data.
findings.evidence: index.js:107-112 computes `iterableIsArray` and calls `this(function_, value, iterableIsArray ? index : undefined)`. readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:29-43 state the mapper receives the item value and its index, equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`. Runtime probe over `new Set(["a", "b", "c"])` printed `["a:undefined","b:undefined","c:undefined"]`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `node --input-type=module` with: import pLimit from "./index.js"; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(await limit.map(new Set(["a", "b", "c"]), (value, index) => `${value}:${String(index)}`)); Expected: `["a:0","b:1","c:2"]`. Actual: `["a:undefined","b:undefined","c:undefined"]`.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass runtime validation
findings.cause: The runtime type check is guarded by the option value itself: `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== "boolean")`, so only truthy invalid values throw.
findings.impact: Invalid options such as `{rejectOnClear: 0}`, `{rejectOnClear: ""}`, or `{rejectOnClear: null}` are silently accepted and treated as disabled. This undermines the documented boolean contract and can hide configuration mistakes in JavaScript callers.
findings.evidence: index.js:12-14 only throws for truthy non-booleans. index.d.ts:99-106 declares `rejectOnClear?: boolean`, and index.test-d.ts:29 only covers the truthy invalid string case. Runtime probe accepted 0, empty string, and null, while throwing only for "nope".
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run `node --input-type=module` with: import pLimit from "./index.js"; for (const rejectOnClear of [0, "", null, "nope"]) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear}); console.log(rejectOnClear, "accepted"); } catch (error) { console.log(rejectOnClear, "threw", error.message); } } Expected: all non-booleans throw. Actual: 0, empty string, and null are accepted.
